title: Implement Self-Service Analytics for Operational and Commercial Teams
narrative: Analytical reporting at FEDC is currently centralised in a data team that builds and maintains reports for operational and commercial stakeholders. Teams submit report requests, which are typically fulfilled within two weeks. This bottleneck means that business questions are answered slowly, and teams use workarounds — manual spreadsheet analysis, shadow data stores — that create data quality and governance risks. We propose implementing a self-service analytics capability that enables operational and commercial teams to query and visualise authorised data without dependency on the central data team. The capability will be built on the existing data warehouse, extended with a semantic layer that exposes business-friendly metrics. Role-based access will ensure teams can only access data appropriate to their function. Training and enablement will be provided to 150 analysts in the first year.

requirements.title: Self-service query capability
requirements.description: Business analysts must be able to build and run reports against authorised data domains without writing SQL or requiring data team assistance for standard query patterns.

requirements.title: Semantic layer
requirements.description: All self-service metrics must be defined in a semantic layer that translates business terminology to underlying data structures, ensuring consistent metric definitions across teams.

requirements.title: Query performance
requirements.description: Self-service queries against datasets of up to 100 million rows must complete within 30 seconds for 95% of executed queries.

recommendations.recommendation: The first requirement uses the phrase **'standard query patterns'** without defining what qualifies. Consider clarifying whether this means predefined report templates, drag-and-drop UI builders, or a specific set of query types — this will help downstream design work.

**'Semantic layer'** is technical jargon. Consider rephrasing to emphasise the business benefit: e.g., *'A business-friendly metrics layer that lets teams use familiar terminology (e.g., "monthly revenue", "customer count") rather than technical database field names'* — this makes the intent clearer for non-technical stakeholders.

The narrative mentions **role-based access** as a key control, but no explicit requirement captures access enforcement. Consider adding a requirement that access controls must be enforced and that unauthorised data access attempts are logged or prevented — this ensures the governance intent is measurable.

Strong overall narrative — clear problem statement, business impact, and scope. The requirement set is testable and well-classified. Minor addition: consider mentioning whether the role-based access model should prevent analysts from accessing certain metrics or only limit row-level data visibility — this distinction will matter for downstream design.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision implements self-service analytics to address a centralised data team bottleneck. This capability directly realises **Data Architecture Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle DAT-PRN-003 (Quality is a producer responsibility) and DAT-PRN-002 (Define once, use everywhere), by requiring a business-friendly semantic layer and ensuring consistent metric definitions across teams.
impact-assessment.impact: Self-service analytics cannot succeed without strong governance of metric definitions and data quality. The proposed semantic layer is a logical control that must be referenced in `DAT-PRN` to enforce consistency. Without explicit principles binding the semantic layer to canonical definitions, teams risk re-creating shadow metrics that undermine the single-source-of-truth intent.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Add a principle to DAT-PRN** that captures the governance model for the semantic layer: e.g., 'All self-service metrics must be defined in a semantic layer that translates to canonical data concepts; metrics not in the semantic layer cannot be queried by business users.' This ensures downstream teams building the self-service platform know their control boundary.
impact-assessment.rationale: Semantic layers are infrastructure; governance principles tell the infrastructure team what rules it must enforce. DAT-PRN is the contract between the architecture and the platform. Without an explicit principle, the semantic layer becomes a technical implementation detail rather than a governed asset, increasing risk of metric proliferation.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision implements a new **self-service analytics capability** using role-based access control (RBAC) to constrain data visibility by business function. This is a new data access pattern not currently represented in **Data Architecture Guardrails** (`DAT-GRD`), which defines non-negotiable enforcement rules for the Data domain.
impact-assessment.impact: Role-based access enforcement at the semantic layer is a guardrail — a mandatory control that prevents unauthorised data visibility. If DAT-GRD does not explicitly require RBAC enforcement and audit logging for self-service queries, downstream teams may implement self-service without the governance safeguards needed to satisfy compliance and risk requirements.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Add a guardrail to DAT-GRD** that mandates: (1) All self-service query access is role-based and linked to business function; (2) Denied or anomalous access attempts are logged; (3) Role-to-data mappings are reviewed quarterly. This makes the control non-negotiable for the platform team.
impact-assessment.rationale: Self-service democratises access; GDPR, data privacy regulations, and internal risk policy require that scale-up in access be matched by scale-up in enforcement visibility. A guardrail signals to the platform team that access control is not optional and must be auditable.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision targets **operational and commercial teams** (approximately 150 analysts) as end-users. No explicit requirement captures enablement or skills, yet the decision narrative emphasises 'training and enablement' as a first-year deliverable. This cross-cuts from Data architecture into **Business Capabilities** — specifically, **Manage Customer Insight** (`CAP-001-03`) and **Manage Finance** (`CAP-009-01`), both of which will consume self-service analytics.
impact-assessment.impact: If the self-service analytics platform is built without coordinating with the skill and organisational readiness of the consuming teams, uptake will be slow. The 150 analysts are internal users of the new capability — they must be trained and their team structures may need to evolve to absorb self-service workflows. This is architectural scope that reaches beyond the Data domain into operating model and business capability delivery.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Review and update BUS-CAP** to reflect the new data analytics workload and skill requirements in the relevant business capabilities — notably `CAP-001-03` (Manage Customer Insight) and `CAP-009-01` (Manage Finance). Consider whether the architecture should reference an enablement artefact (e.g. a new role taxonomy or skill matrix) that links the platform capability to the people and teams that operate it. Current artefact types do not capture enablement; if needed, flag as a future artefact-type addition.
impact-assessment.rationale: Business capabilities describe *what the business does*, including how it deploys its people. Self-service analytics redistributes capability ownership away from the central data team to business teams. The BUS-CAP model should reflect that shift, making it visible in executive reviews that the organisation must actively build new skills in 150 users.

impact-assessment.finding: The self-service platform will operate alongside the existing data warehouse and will require **Application Domains & Platforms** (`APP-DAP`) updates. The decision scope statement names `DAT-PRN`, but the semantic layer and query interface are applications — they sit in **APP-DOM-DATA** (Data & Analytics domain) under **PLAT-BI** (BI & Analytics platform, lifecycle: adopt) and **PLAT-DATA-LAKEHOUSE** (Data Lakehouse, lifecycle: adopt).
impact-assessment.impact: If APP-DAP is not updated to explicitly capture the semantic layer as a platform component or service, the Application architecture will not reflect the new logical separation between raw data (lakehouse) and business-friendly query surface (semantic layer). This can lead to downstream platform teams treating the semantic layer as configuration rather than as a distinct architectural element with its own governance and evolution path.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Add or update APP-DAP** to capture the semantic layer as either: (1) a new platform under APP-DOM-DATA (e.g., `PLAT-SEMANTIC-LAYER`), or (2) an explicit sub-component or service within `PLAT-BI` or `PLAT-DATA-LAKEHOUSE`. Document its type (system-of-insight or system-of-record) and lifecycle intent (adopt). Ensure **Application Architecture Principles** (`APP-PRN`) includes guidance on how semantic layers relate to the broader Application landscape (e.g., do they expose stable APIs? are they versioned?).
impact-assessment.rationale: Application architecture tracks the platforms that realise data capabilities. The semantic layer is not a data artefact — it is an application that sits between the user and the warehouse. Treating it explicitly in APP-DAP makes it visible for capacity planning, dependency management, and vendor/platform evolution decisions.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision narrative states that self-service will address 'standard query patterns' but does not define what these are. **Data Architecture Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) and **Data Architecture Strategy** (`DAT-STR`) together set the foundation for what the data platform supports; without alignment on 'standard' patterns, the semantic layer risks becoming a dumping ground for every ad-hoc query shape that consuming teams demand, undermining the governance intent of the semantic layer.
impact-assessment.impact: Scope creep on the semantic layer is common in self-service analytics projects. Without principle-driven constraints, the platform team will face pressure to expose new metrics and query patterns for every business team request, leading to a fragmented, unsustainable semantic layer and delaying or degrading the 30-second query performance target for large datasets.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Clarify and document 'standard query patterns' as part of the ADR resolution**: document in `DAT-PRN` what query shapes the semantic layer will support (e.g., 'filtered aggregations over up to 3 dimensions') and what it will not (e.g., 'freeform exploratory SQL'). This becomes a governance rule that the platform team can enforce. If 'standard patterns' are already defined elsewhere, reference them; if not, define them before platform build begins.
impact-assessment.rationale: Governance is most effective when rules are precise and enforceable. Semantic layers without constraints become maintenance nightmares. A principle that defines the boundary of 'standard' is a design input to the platform team and a deflection mechanism for out-of-scope requests.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 directly advances **Data Strategy** (`DAT-STR`) statement *'Default to self-service; specialist data teams support domains, not gate them'* (DAT-STR-003). The self-service analytics capability shifts the operating model from ticket-based report delivery (centralised data team) to autonomous querying by business analysts, eliminating the bottleneck identified in the decision narrative.
strategy-alignment.impact: This decision realises the medium-term target outcome of DAT-STR-003 ('80% of analytics use cases satisfied without bespoke pipeline work'). By enabling operational and commercial teams to build and run reports without data team assistance, the decision frees specialist capacity to focus on platform improvements and data governance — a direct strategic gain.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Ensure the implementation plan explicitly measures progress toward the DAT-STR-003 target. Define metrics: e.g., percentage of analytics queries served by self-service vs. bespoke work, and the reallocation of data team capacity to platform and governance work. Document these in the project charter.
strategy-alignment.rationale: DAT-STR-003 is a strategic shift from request-driven to platform-driven delivery. Explicit metrics tie the decision outcome to the strategic objective and help track whether the implementation is achieving the intended operating-model change.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 advances **Data Strategy** statement *'Federate data ownership to domain teams; centralise only standards and platform'* (DAT-STR-002). The semantic layer acts as a centralised standard (business-friendly metrics defined once) while empowering domain teams (operational and commercial analysts) to consume and query those metrics autonomously, implementing the federated-ownership model.
strategy-alignment.impact: The decision distributes analytics capability away from the central data team, aligning with the medium-term target of DAT-STR-002 ('Every data product has a named domain owner; a single self-service platform with shared standards by 2026'). This reduces bottleneck risk and improves time-to-insight for consuming teams.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Define and document the data ownership boundaries: which metrics belong to which domain, and who (in each domain) is accountable for metric definition and quality. Link this explicitly to the semantic layer design — ensure the semantic layer's structure reflects domain ownership, not a flat, undifferentiated metric repository.
strategy-alignment.rationale: Federated ownership only works if domains are clearly delineated. The semantic layer is the governance mechanism; its structure and metadata must encode ownership, so consuming teams know whom to contact for metric changes.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 strongly advances **Business Strategy** statement *'Decide with data — every material business decision must cite the evidence that supports it'* (BUS-STR-003). The self-service analytics capability directly realises the target outcome of BUS-STR-003 ('Self-serve analytics available to every team'), by enabling 150 analysts in operational and commercial functions to query and visualise authorised data independently.
strategy-alignment.impact: This decision removes a structural barrier to evidence-driven decision-making: slow analytics turnaround. By reducing the time from question to insight (from two weeks to real-time query execution), the decision increases the likelihood that teams will cite data in decisions, advancing the strategic objective of BUS-STR-003.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Include in the project communications an emphasis on *decision-making speed* as the business benefit. When training the 150 analysts, highlight that self-service enables faster evidence gathering and thus faster, better decisions. Track adoption through decision logs and team surveys to measure whether the capability is being used as intended.
strategy-alignment.rationale: BUS-STR-003 is not just about analytics access; it is about behaviour change — making data-driven decision-making the norm. The self-service platform is enabling infrastructure; adoption and behaviour change are the strategic outcomes. Explicit focus on decision-making speed reinforces the strategic intent.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 advances **Business Strategy** statement *'Build digital-by-default operations — paper, manual handovers, and bespoke spreadsheets are exceptions, not the norm'* (BUS-STR-005). The decision narrative explicitly identifies shadow data stores and manual spreadsheet analysis as current workarounds; the self-service analytics capability replaces these with a governed, digital analytics platform.
strategy-alignment.impact: This decision directly addresses the operational inefficiency identified in BUS-STR-005. By moving analytical work from spreadsheets to a managed platform, the decision contributes to the target outcome ('Top 20 business processes fully digital end-to-end by 2026') and reduces data quality and governance risks created by shadow systems.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: As part of project scope, explicitly plan the migration of current spreadsheet-based reports into the self-service semantic layer. Document which spreadsheets are in scope and estimate the effort to formalise their metrics. This makes the shift from manual to digital visible and measurable.
strategy-alignment.rationale: Digital-by-default is achieved through deliberate migration, not by waiting for natural adoption. Explicit scope and tracking ensure that the self-service platform displaces shadow systems rather than existing alongside them.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 does not explicitly address **Data Strategy** principle *'Privacy and consent are designed in, not bolted on'* (DAT-STR-004). The decision narrative mentions role-based access control but does not emphasise privacy design (e.g., personal data minimisation, consent traceability, or privacy-aware semantic layer design).
strategy-alignment.impact: Self-service analytics at scale expands data access to 150 new users. Without explicit privacy design, the platform risks creating compliance gaps: unauthorised exposure of personal data, inadequate consent records, or inability to trace which users accessed what data. This is a material gap given FEDC's regulatory environment.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Add a requirement to the decision: 'The semantic layer must implement privacy-by-design principles, including (1) personal data classification in the semantic model; (2) consent-linked data masking or filtering; (3) audit logging of all access to personal data.' Reference DAT-STR-004 explicitly in the design brief to signal that privacy is non-negotiable, not an afterthought.
strategy-alignment.rationale: DAT-STR-004 is short-term (horizon: short-term), making it a near-term priority. Self-service analytics must be designed with privacy from the start, not retrofitted later. Explicit requirement language ensures the platform team knows this is a strategic design input, not a compliance checklist item.

referential-integrity.finding: **Data Architecture Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle references are sound. DAT-PRN-003 and DAT-PRN-002 both exist and are correctly identified in the impact assessment. All principle IDs resolve to defined entities.
referential-integrity.impact: The decision's citation of existing principles ensures architecture traceability and evidence-based recommendations.
referential-integrity.recommendation: No action required — all Data Architecture Principles citations resolve correctly.
referential-integrity.rationale: Referential integrity for principles validates that the decision is grounded in established governance, not inventing new rules.

referential-integrity.finding: **Data Architecture Guardrails** (`DAT-GRD`) is referenced in the impact-assessment section with a recommendation to add guardrails for self-service access control, but the current `DAT-GRD` catalogue at `architectures/clients/fedc/1.0.0/domains/data/physical/DAT-GRD.json` contains an empty `guardrails` array. The catalogue structure exists, but no guardrail entities are defined.
referential-integrity.impact: The absence of defined guardrails means the recommended control ('All self-service query access is role-based...') cannot yet be referenced. Until guardrails are added to the `DAT-GRD` catalogue, downstream teams will lack an authoritative source for mandatory Data domain enforcement rules.
referential-integrity.recommendation: As part of ADR-013 resolution, add the recommended guardrails to `DAT-GRD`: (1) self-service query access is role-based and linked to business function; (2) denied or anomalous access attempts are logged; (3) role-to-data mappings are reviewed quarterly. Once added, update the impact-assessment section to reference the new guardrail IDs.
referential-integrity.rationale: Guardrails are enforceable rules, not aspirational statements. Referential integrity requires that every guardrail cited in architecture decisions points to a defined entity in the authoritative catalogue, so platform teams know which rules to implement.

referential-integrity.finding: **Business Capabilities** (`BUS-CAP`) references are sound. Capabilities `CAP-001-03` (Manage Customer Insight) and `CAP-009-01` (Manage Finance) both exist at level 2, with valid parent IDs (`CAP-001` and `CAP-009` respectively). All parent references resolve correctly.
referential-integrity.impact: The decision's identification of consuming business capabilities ensures the self-service analytics capability is explicitly linked to the business functions it enables.
referential-integrity.recommendation: No action required — all Business Capabilities citations resolve correctly.
referential-integrity.rationale: Linking architectural decisions to business capabilities ensures decisions are traceable to business outcomes and prevents orphaned capabilities.

referential-integrity.finding: **Application Domains & Platforms** (`APP-DAP`) references are sound. Domain `APP-DOM-DATA`, platform `PLAT-BI`, and platform `PLAT-DATA-LAKEHOUSE` all exist with correct domain-id references. All platform-to-domain associations are valid.
referential-integrity.impact: The decision's identification of the application platforms enables downstream teams to understand the technology scope and evolution path for self-service analytics.
referential-integrity.recommendation: No action required — all Application Domains & Platforms citations resolve correctly.
referential-integrity.rationale: Platform references ensure decisions connect architectural decisions to the concrete systems that realise them.

referential-integrity.finding: **Integrity summary:** All references to defined entities in `DAT-PRN`, `BUS-CAP`, and `APP-DAP` resolve correctly. The single integrity issue is that `DAT-GRD` (the catalogue where guardrails live) is structurally present but currently empty. The impact-assessment makes a valid recommendation to populate it, which resolves the integrity gap.
referential-integrity.impact: The decision can proceed with the understanding that the recommended guardrails must be added to `DAT-GRD` during resolution in order for platform teams to have an authoritative reference.
referential-integrity.recommendation: Treat the addition of guardrails to `DAT-GRD` as part of the ADR-013 resolution workflow. Once guardrails are added, verify their IDs against the impact-assessment recommendations.
referential-integrity.rationale: Referential integrity is achieved when every reference points to a defined entity and every required entity is defined. This decision's recommendations create the missing entity (guardrails), so integrity will be established during resolution.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Define once, use everywhere'* (DAT-PRN-002) is **adhered to**. The decision explicitly mandates a semantic layer that 'translates business terminology to underlying data structures, ensuring consistent metric definitions across teams.' This centralised, canonical definition is the core mechanism for enforcing DAT-PRN-002.
principles-alignment.impact: Adherence to DAT-PRN-002 is critical to the decision's success. Without a single, authoritative semantic layer, consuming teams will create parallel metric definitions, fragmenting the self-service platform and undermining the governance intent.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Document in the implementation plan how the semantic layer will enforce the 'define once' principle: e.g., metadata governance controls that prevent teams from creating custom metric definitions outside the semantic layer, audit trails for metric changes, and a review process for new metrics.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-002 exists to prevent silent divergence. The self-service analytics capability scales the number of metric consumers from a few (data team) to 150 (operational and commercial analysts). Without strict 'define once' enforcement, the platform will degrade into a fragmented metrics repository.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Quality is a producer responsibility'* (DAT-PRN-003) is **adhered to**. The decision narrative states that 'teams can only access data appropriate to their function' through role-based access, and the semantic layer mediates access to 'authorised data.' This positions the data producer (centralised platform) as responsible for quality and access governance, not the consuming analyst.
principles-alignment.impact: Adherence ensures that data quality expectations are explicitly owned by the platform team, not pushed downstream to consumers. This prevents the common self-service anti-pattern of 'consumers re-cleanse data at query time.'
principles-alignment.recommendation: Include in the semantic layer design a quality attestation model: each metric exposed via the semantic layer must have a defined SLA (e.g., refresh frequency, expected completeness). Document quality issues and escalation paths in the platform runbook.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-003 protects against distributed quality debt. As the platform scales to 150 users, the producer must own quality explicitly, or the platform becomes a distribution mechanism for data-quality problems.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Privacy by design'* (DAT-PRN-004) is **silent — a material gap**. The decision narrative mentions role-based access control but does not address personal-data classification, consent traceability, or privacy-aware semantic layer design. This is a critical silence given the scale (150 new users) and regulatory environment.
principles-alignment.impact: The silence creates a compliance risk. Self-service analytics at scale expands data access without explicit privacy-design controls. Consumers may unknowingly access personal data without knowing consent constraints, and the platform lacks audit trails for personal-data access. This violates the principle's core intent ('privacy from capture, not retrofitted').
principles-alignment.recommendation: Add explicit privacy-design requirements to the decision: (1) personal-data fields are classified in the semantic layer; (2) consent-linked masking or filtering is applied at query time; (3) all access to personal data is audited; (4) the semantic layer design document includes a privacy threat model. Reference DAT-PRN-004 by ID to signal that privacy is non-negotiable.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-004 is short-term strategic priority. Self-service analytics makes privacy-design decisions visible to 150 users; if privacy is not designed in from the start, compliance retrofits will be expensive and incomplete.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Every data domain has an owner'* (DAT-PRN-001) is **silent**. The decision narrative does not identify who owns the semantic layer itself or who is accountable for its metrics, definitions, and lifecycle. While the semantic layer is governance infrastructure (centralised), the principle requires that 'each data domain in DAT-DAC has a single accountable steward.'
principles-alignment.impact: The silence creates ambiguity about accountability. If the semantic layer is viewed as a shared utility with no clear owner, disputes over metric definitions will lack an escalation path and changes will be slow or contested.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Before platform build begins, define the semantic layer ownership model: Is it owned by the central data team, or by a rotating domain steward? Document who is accountable for metric definitions, change review, and SLA compliance. Link this explicitly to the ADR resolution and to the data governance working group.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-001 recognises that unowned data drifts in quality and meaning. A semantic layer is owned data infrastructure; without clear stewardship, it will become unmaintainable or untrustworthy.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Open contracts, open standards'* (DAT-PRN-005) is **implicitly adhered to** but not explicitly documented. The decision does not specify the technical format or interface for the semantic layer (e.g., API, SQL interface, JSON Schema), so it is unclear whether the 'open contracts' principle will be satisfied in implementation.
principles-alignment.impact: If the semantic layer implementation uses proprietary or undocumented query formats, downstream consumers (analysts and other applications) will be locked into the platform, reducing reuse and limiting vendor portability.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Document in the design brief that the semantic layer's query interface must be schema-documented and standards-based (e.g., SQL, GraphQL, or REST with OpenAPI). Require the platform team to publish the semantic layer's contract before implementation. This makes DAT-PRN-005 enforceable.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-005 prevents vendor and format lock-in. At self-service scale, many consumers will depend on the semantic layer's interface; locking them into a proprietary format is a long-term operational risk.

principles-alignment.finding: **Business Principles** (`BUS-PRN`) principle *'Process digital by default'* (BUS-PRN-006) is **strongly adhered to**. The decision explicitly addresses shadow spreadsheet analysis and manual workarounds as the current state problem; the self-service analytics capability moves analytical work from spreadsheets and manual processes to a governed digital platform.
principles-alignment.impact: Strong alignment with BUS-PRN-006 increases the likelihood of adoption and operational efficiency. By removing the spreadsheet friction point, the decision removes a barrier to digital-by-default operations.
principles-alignment.recommendation: In project communications and rollout, explicitly link the self-service platform to the BUS-PRN-006 strategic objective. When training the 150 analysts, highlight that self-service replaces manual spreadsheet work with governed, auditable analytics. Track spreadsheet displacement as a success metric.
principles-alignment.rationale: BUS-PRN-006 drives digital excellence. Self-service analytics is a concrete realisation of the principle; making this explicit in communications reinforces the strategic intent.

principles-alignment.finding: **Application Principles** (`APP-PRN`) principle *'Observability is built in, not bolted on'* (APP-PRN-005) is **silent**. The decision does not specify that the self-service platform will include observability (health checks, structured logs, metrics, traces) from day one. This is material because consumption patterns and query performance are critical to the success and operations of the platform.
principles-alignment.impact: Without built-in observability, the operations team will lack visibility into query patterns, performance degradation, and user adoption. Troubleshooting will be slow, and the platform will be difficult to scale as analytics volume grows.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Add a non-functional requirement to the decision: 'The self-service platform must expose health endpoints, structure logs in machine-readable format, emit RED metrics (request rate, error rate, duration) for all queries, and support distributed tracing. Observability must be configured and tested before production launch.'
principles-alignment.rationale: APP-PRN-005 is a non-negotiable quality standard for applications. The semantic layer and query interface are applications; without observability built in from day one, operations teams will be flying blind, increasing the risk of outages and degraded user experience.
